title: Big O: how work grows
summary: A way to describe how much slower code gets as the input grows, so you can tell a fast idea from a slow one before you run it.

sections.heading: Count steps, not seconds
body: Timing code depends on the computer. Instead, count roughly how many steps it takes for an input of size `n`, and watch what happens when `n` grows.

One loop over the input takes about `n` steps: O(n). A loop inside a loop takes about `n × n`: O(n²). Ten times more input means ten times more work for the first, and a hundred times more for the second.

sections.heading: The common shapes, fastest first
body: - **O(1)**: the same work whatever the size. Reading `arr[5]`, looking up a key in a map.
- **O(log n)**: halve the problem each step. Binary search.
- **O(n)**: touch each item once. One loop.
- **O(n log n)**: good sorting algorithms. Usually what `sort` costs.
- **O(n²)**: compare every item with every other. A loop inside a loop.
- **O(2ⁿ)**: try every combination. Fine for 20 items, hopeless for 60.

sections.heading: Why halving is so powerful
body: Halving a million over and over reaches 1 in under 20 steps. That is why binary search and balanced trees stay fast on huge inputs.

javascript.code:
let n = 1000000
let steps = 0
while (n > 1) {
  n = Math.floor(n / 2)
  steps++
}
console.log(steps)

python.code:
n = 1000000
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n //= 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)

sections.heading: Hidden loops
body: Some one-word operations are loops in disguise. Put one inside your own loop and an O(n) idea quietly becomes O(n²):
- `shift`/`unshift` in JavaScript, `pop(0)`/`insert(0, x)` in Python: move every item.
The usual fix is a set or map for lookups, and a pointer or index instead of removing from the front.

mistakes: Thinking a short line is a cheap line. `arr.includes(x)` is a whole loop.
Worrying about small constant factors before fixing an O(n²) that should be O(n).
Forgetting that recursion without memoization can be exponential.
